questions.q: Why does the summary say negative events affect us more strongly than positive ones?
a: Our brains evolved to treat possible threats as survival risks
We encounter far more bad events than good ones
Positive events are usually less memorable
Society trains us to expect the worst outcome
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains the negativity bias as a leftover from a time when most threats could kill us.

questions.q: What does a sad amygdala tend to do?
a: Release stress hormones and drive fearful reactions
Boost motivation, ambition and optimism
Store positive memories for later recall
Slow the brain's ability to learn new skills
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts the sad amygdala, which releases cortisol and adrenaline, with the happy one.

questions.q: How does the Good Year Box practice work?
a: You write down one good thing each night and keep it in a box
You fill a box with gifts to open at the end of the year
You draw a yearly goal from a box each morning
You collect photos of happy events and review them monthly
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes reviewing the day before bed, noting one positive event on paper and placing it in a box.

questions.q: Which three sources of positive experience does the summary name?
a: Happy memories, small details and generosity
Exercise, healthy food and enough sleep
Friendship, travel and creative work
Meditation, journaling and solitude
questions.why: Lesson 3 lists dwelling on a happy memory, noticing a small good detail and being generous toward others.

questions.q: What does the summary say about the brain's capacity to change?
a: It keeps growing, so negativity bias can be rewired
It stops developing once childhood ends
It changes only through medication or therapy
It resists change after repeated negative experiences
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the brain never stops growing, so regular positive experiences can tone down the sad amygdala.
